96 Plus, more housing means cooler rents, bipartisan tax hate, and AI after the Riemann Hypothesis   Is this email difficult to read? View in browser                 Greg Ip   Is Nvidia Becoming a Government-Sponsored Enterprise?   Plus, more housing means cooler rents, bipartisan tax hate, and AI after the Riemann Hypothesis   Nvidia had long exemplified the blurred line between boardroom and state under President Trump. Now that it has rehired Jensen Huang as chief executive under pressure from Trump, the line has all but disappeared, leaving Nvidia for now effectively a government-sponsored enterprise.

   Nvidia’s board said it rehired Huang after getting assurances that he wasn’t a national security risk, and Trump said the Justice Department knew of no unlawful conduct.

   Like the original government-sponsored enterprises, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, Nvidia’s mission and governance are now effectively steered by the federal government. Huang owes his job to Trump.

   The episode underscores how Trump can use the federal government’s vast influence over corporations, either through regulation or law enforcement, to exact cooperation. Just last year, he called on Intel to fire its CEO over ties to China, then relented after the company granted the federal government a 10% stake.

   Nvidia’s legal shield is good for only as long as Trump is willing and able to provide it. Investigations still surround Huang and the company. Peter Harrell, an attorney specializing in international finance who advised former President Joe Biden, notes the Justice Department, perhaps under a future administration, could still prosecute Nvidia. The company may thus seek a settlement now. Or, Harrell said, Trump may pardon the company.

   These are my key takeaways.

   State capitalism stays alive. Huang had personally lobbied Trump to sell chips to China. Trump agreed, in return for a cut of chip sales. By aligning its interests so closely with Trump, Nvidia became the poster child for America’s drift into state capitalism (and created the conditions for the current scandal).

   Last week I speculated that the scandal might halt the drift toward state capitalism . That now looks premature, but the story isn’t over.

   A setback for China hawks. Nvidia divided the Trump administration’s China hawks—like Secretary of State Marco Rubio and, more recently, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who want to deprive China of the most advanced U.S. tech—from doves like Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who want to wring as much money from China as possible. Hawks seized on Huang’s downfall to push through tougher controls on chip exports. His return is a setback.

   But not defeat. Huang could yet persuade Trump to weaken those new controls, or look the other way as customers circumvent them. That may be hard given his diminished standing. Moreover, the mood in Congress has shifted. Republican Senate hawks such as Tom Cotton (Ark.) and John Kennedy (La.) have turned critical of Lutnick and Huang. Come January, Democrats plan sweeping investigations of the ties between Trump and Silicon Valley.

   Bipartisan support is growing for attaching tougher export controls to must-pass defense funding. Still, Eddie Fishman of the Council on Foreign Relations notes enforcement is up to the administration: “If tech companies think they can make decisions that undermine U.S. national security with no repercussions, even more stringent export control laws may not materially affect their corporate decision-making.”

   The markets are the ultimate arbiter. Huang mattered to Trump not just because of his importance to AI, but to the stock market. “Investors should be very happy,” Trump told CNBC Monday as the market roared back.

   His administration regularly chooses to manage markets rather than the root problems disturbing those markets. When bond yields were rising because of inflation and deficits, Bessent responded by buying back some longer-dated issues. When oil prices spiked because of the war with Iran, Trump repeatedly talked them down with promises of ceasefires and victories that never happened.

   The shadow over AI remains. Just as such interventions didn’t solve the underlying problems with the bond and oil markets, they will not lift the cloud over AI. Demand for Nvidia chips and computing power has been driven by hyperscalers such as Alphabet, Meta and SpaceX and frontier labs like Anthropic, financed not by commercial revenue but the debt markets and by Nvidia itself. Huang’s return won’t resolve doubts about the sustainability of that investment.

Whether you’re upgrading your home setup or shopping for early gifts, explore our roundup featuring top savings from Breville, Apple, and more.   SHOP  >       What I’m Following   Increase housing, watch rents respond. The public always seems skeptical that more housing will lower costs, so it helps to have success stories. The Pew Charitable Trusts reports on one : In 2021-22, Raleigh, N.C., rolled back limits on density and regulated by lot size and building height instead; made it easier to build “plexes” of a few units, tiny homes and townhomes; allowed higher density near transit stops; and abolished citywide parking minimums. The result: Between 2021 and 2024, Raleigh’s housing stock grew 8%, faster than in North Carolina or the country, but rents grew by less than in the state or country, even as the city’s population outstripped the state and country.

   Do Republicans really hate taxes more than Democrats do? Maybe not. Asked to guess in a survey, Republican voters would be more likely than Democratic voters to appeal against their property taxes. But in fact, voters of both parties file tax appeals at similar rates . Brad Nathan of Rutgers Business School and two co-authors published their findings in a new study that matched up property-tax rolls and voting records in Dallas County, Texas. “Despite differing tax policy preferences and public perceptions about their behavior, Democrats and Republicans are strikingly similar in both their propensity to appeal their property taxes and their underlying motives,” they write.

   AI solved the Riemann Hypothesis . So? On X, journalist Derek Thompson writes, “You really cannot get a cleaner example of the principle that ‘AI capabilities ≠ real-world AI consequences’” than the contrast between the breakthrough by Anthropic’s AI and the broad-based selloff in AI stocks (including Anthropic). His hypothesis is that these models’ otherworldly powers have vastly overstated , in our minds, how much everyday value they’ll have. Indeed, there are many examples of a technology’s raw power overstating its actual usefulness, including atomic energy, whose destructive potential proved to be a major constraint on its diffusion. In financial-market terms, this may explain why shares of Apple, the big-tech company that has invested least in AI, are down so much less, and why AI equities have been more resilient than AI bonds. “Solving an old pure math problem does not immediately widen Anthropic’s operating margins,” Séb Krier, a senior staff research scientist at Google DeepMind, writes on X . It could mean AI will become commoditized, hurting those margins.

       More From WSJ     CARLOS BARRIA/REUTERS   • Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick sometimes meets Trump at the White House for off-the-books meetings after staff have gone home for the night, according to officials familiar with the matter. 

   • The most worrisome part of the Nvidia scandal? “The suggestion that one of the most valuable, most important companies was conducting major deals between suppliers and customers on handshake agreements with [Jensen] Huang ,” my colleague Tim Higgins writes.

   • “My mom and dad basically didn’t plan very well for anything that was going to happen to them in the future,” says 49-year-old Natalie Rodrigues. As for many Americans, caring for her aging parents has upended Rodrigues’s own financial plans.

       What to Watch   Tuesday 

   • 10 a.m. ET: The Conference Board’s consumer-confidence index is expected to show that shoppers’ spirits improved this month. The University of Michigan’s parallel survey showed the same last week.

   Wednesday 

   • 8:30 a.m. ET: Economists estimate that the Fed’s preferred inflation metric, the PCE price index, was up by 0.3% excluding food and energy last month. That would likely raise the 12-month core PCE inflation rate to 3.2%, underscoring the central bank’s inflation challenge.

   Thursday 

   • Happy Thanksgiving. U.S. markets will be closed, and we’ll take a day off from the newsletter. See you next week.

       Thoughts on today’s newsletter? Or on the wider world? Please share them with me at wsjeconomics@wsj.com . 

       What I’m Reading   • “An Illinois grocery store funded by state and federal tax dollars closed abruptly…a little more than a year after its grand opening, serving as a potential warning sign to Democrats pushing for more government-funded food stores.” ( The Washington Times )

   • “Even moderate candidates won their midterm elections by talking about economic inequality and billionaires, suggesting the distinction between Democratic Party factions may be softening…Leftist groups still find themselves divided over identity and privilege,” Meagan Day writes. ( New York Times Opinion )

   • “The Fed’s 2% inflation ambition is misguided…3% inflation is a more realistic ambition in the new world.” ( Bill Ackman )

       About Me   I’m The Wall Street Journal’s chief economics commentator. I’ve been writing about economics, markets and politics for more than 40 years, in the U.S. and from around the world.
